overview.title: 📖 Overview: When Did the Blemish Come First?
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 14a–14b
overview.hebrewSource: שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא טָפֵל חָמוּר מִן הָעִיקָּר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: A new mishna draws a sharp line between two kinds of blemished consecrated animals: those blemished before consecration, which never carry inherent sanctity and are only sanctified in value, and those blemished after consecration, which remain fully sanctified despite the blemish. The Gemara traces the far-reaching consequences of that distinction — for firstborn status, priestly gifts, shearing and labor, offspring, substitutes, and burial after death — and along the way works through a five-candidate chain of possibilities for a single verse in Deuteronomy before settling on its true subject: the prohibition against sacrificing a blemished animal on a private altar.

slides.title: 🐑 Two Categories of Once-Blemished Consecrated Animals
slides.subtitle: The order of blemish and consecration changes everything

boxes.title: Blemish Preceded Consecration
items: Only value is sanctified, never the body itself
After redemption: subject to firstborn law and priestly gifts; may be sheared and worked
Slaughtered outside the Temple: no liability; creates no substitute
If it dies: may still be redeemed and fed to dogs

boxes.title: Consecration Preceded Blemish
items: The animal itself was once fully, inherently sanctified
Even after redemption: exempt from firstborn law and priestly gifts; may not be sheared or worked
Slaughtered outside the Temple: liable for karet; does create a substitute
If it dies: must be buried, not redeemed

slides.title: 📜 Chasing a Verse Through Five Candidates
slides.subtitle: What does 'you shall not sacrifice a blemished ox or sheep' (Deuteronomy 17:1) really teach?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Elazar: it teaches that slaughtering a blemished animal on a permitted private altar violates a prohibition
2️⃣ Why not apply it to a firstborn instead? Rejected — a firstborn's blemish-disqualification is already explicit elsewhere (Deuteronomy 15:21)
3️⃣ Or to animal tithe? Rejected — already derived by verbal analogy ('passing') from the firstborn's own rule
4️⃣ Or to a substitute (temurah) animal? Rejected — already derived from 'it and its substitute' (Leviticus 27:10)

5️⃣ Rabbi Zeira: apply it to the offspring of consecrated animals instead! Rava counters: the school of Rabbi Yishmael already derives that from a separate verse — confirming the verse means the private altar after all

slides.title: 🐣 Can a Newborn Be Redeemed While Still Unblemished?
slides.subtitle: A baraita's answer, and its logical limit

nodes.content: ❓ The offspring of a blemished, value-consecrated mother (conceived before her redemption) — must it wait for its own blemish before redemption, like offspring of an inherently sanctified mother?
📜 Baraita: one who dedicates permanently blemished animals for the altar — if they give birth, the offspring may be sold and redeemed without needing a blemish
✅ Reasoning: 'the subsidiary should not be more severe than the primary' — the mother herself never carried inherent sanctity, so neither can her offspring
⚖️ Contrast: if one deliberately consecrates an unblemished male animal 'for its value,' Rava rules it DOES receive full inherent sanctity — there is no subsidiary relationship limiting it

slides.title: ⚰️ If a Consecrated Animal Dies Before Redemption
slides.subtitle: Does 'standing and valuation' apply to every consecrated animal?

lines.speaker: R' Shimon
lines.text: Animals consecrated for Temple maintenance (like a red heifer) were never subject to 'standing and valuation' — so even after death, they may still be redeemed and fed to dogs. The same applies to any animal blemished from the outset.

lines.speaker: Source
lines.text: Proven from the doubled word 'אוֹתָהּ / אוֹתָהּ' (Leviticus 27:11–12), which excludes an animal blemished from the start from that requirement.

lines.speaker: School of Levi
lines.text: Disagree — all consecrated animals, even undomesticated ones or birds that could never be sacrificed, were included in 'standing and valuation.' Once dead, they must be buried.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But then what do they do with that same exclusionary word 'אוֹתָהּ'? The Gemara concedes this reading is difficult for the school of Levi's position, and leaves it open.

slides.title: 🔥 When Does an Animal 'Make' a Substitute?
slides.subtitle: Only what was itself sanctified can pass sanctity onward
rows: Good and unblemished from the start, later disqualified
Yes — 'he shall not exchange a good for a bad' implies a good original animal does create sanctity in its substitute
Blemished from the very outset (never inherently sanctified)
No — since the animal itself never carried inherent sanctity, nothing transfers to a proposed substitute

callout.label: The daf's throughline:
callout.text: What an animal never itself acquired, it cannot pass on — not to its offspring, and not to its substitute.

summary.principle: Whether a consecrated animal's blemish came before or after its consecration determines everything downstream — its firstborn and gift obligations, its offspring's status, its ability to create a substitute, and whether it may be redeemed after death — because subsidiary sanctity can never exceed its source.

flowSteps.content: 🐑 A blemish before consecration means only value-sanctity; a blemish after means the animal remains inherently sanctified
📜 Deuteronomy 17:1's prohibition on sacrificing a blemished animal is chased through five candidates before landing on the private altar

columns.content: 🐣 A blemished mother's offspring may be redeemed unblemished — subsidiary sanctity can't outrank the source
⚰️ Rabbi Shimon and the school of Levi dispute whether all consecrated animals need 'standing and valuation'

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only an animal that itself carried inherent sanctity can pass that status to its offspring or its substitute

quiz.q: According to the mishna, what is the status of offspring conceived before redemption, born to an animal whose blemish preceded its consecration?
o: Forbidden, just like offspring of an inherently sanctified animal
Permitted, since the mother only ever had sanctity that inheres in value, never inherent sanctity
Their status depends on the offspring's own appearance
They must be sacrificed on the altar
quiz.e: Because the mother's sanctity was only monetary (she was blemished before consecration), her offspring, even if conceived before her redemption, are permitted.

quiz.q: Why does the Gemara reject applying Deuteronomy 17:1 ('you shall not sacrifice a blemished ox or sheep') to the case of a firstborn animal?
o: Because firstborns are never blemished
Because a firstborn's disqualification due to blemish is already stated explicitly in a different verse (Deuteronomy 15:19-21)
Because firstborns are not subject to any blemish laws
Because the Gemara accepts this reading
quiz.e: Since the Torah already states explicitly elsewhere that a blemished firstborn may not be sacrificed, Deuteronomy 17:1 must be teaching a different halakha — ultimately, the private altar.

quiz.q: According to the baraita's reasoning, why can the offspring of a permanently blemished, value-consecrated animal be redeemed even while itself unblemished?
o: Because all offspring may always be redeemed immediately
Because 'the subsidiary should not be more severe than the primary' — the mother herself never had inherent sanctity, so neither does the offspring
Because offspring are never subject to consecration
Because the Torah explicitly permits it by name
quiz.e: The principle is that a secondary consecration (the offspring's) cannot be stricter than the primary consecration (the mother's), which was only monetary to begin with.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Shimon, why can animals blemished from the outset still be redeemed even after they die, unlike ordinary sacrificial animals?
o: Because dead animals are always redeemable
Because they were never included in the Torah's 'standing and valuation' requirement, derived from the doubled word 'otah'
Because Rabbi Shimon rejects all redemption laws
Because only birds require standing and valuation
quiz.e: Rabbi Shimon derives from the repeated word 'otah' in Leviticus 27:11-12 that animals blemished from the outset (and Temple-maintenance items) are excluded from the standing-and-valuation requirement, which normally demands a live animal be presented to a priest.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara, does an animal that was blemished from the very outset create sanctity in an animal substituted for it?
o: Yes, all consecrated animals create valid substitutes
No — only an animal that was itself good and unblemished at the outset creates sanctity in its substitute
It depends on the substitute's own blemish status
The question is left completely unaddressed
quiz.e: The verse 'he shall not exchange a good for a bad' implies that only a fundamentally good (unblemished) original animal can transfer sanctity to a substitute; one blemished from the start cannot, since it never possessed inherent sanctity itself.
